To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
“A systematic review of 84 sources, emanating from 27 countries, identified 11 quality domains and 58 criteria concepts related to user-facing eHealth program evaluations.”

1) there is an increasing amount of published criteria related to the evaluation and development of user-facing ehealth products, and that 2) the criteria can be grouped into 11 domains that can be further grouped into 58 criteria concepts.
1) 454 criteria were extracted from 84 sources, 2) 11 quality domains were created, 3) 58 criteria concepts were identified, and 4) 134 concepts’ subgroup were created.
In summary, our research is concerned with
identifying and classifying key criteria concepts that are relevant for the evaluation of user-faced eHealth products.
the identification of key quality criteria related to the evaluation and design of user-facing ehealth programs.
the identification of key quality criteria concepts for the evaluation of eHealth products.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the quality of mHealth and ehealth products is evaluated using 11 quality domains and 58 quality concepts.

the evaluation of user facing eHealth products should be based on a set of criteria related to the following domains: usability, visual design, user engagement, content, persuasive design, social presence, therapeutic alliance, credibility/accountability, classification, privacy/security and, lastly, a domain that encompasses the remaining criteria that do not fit within the other 10 domains.
the evaluation criteria for user-facing eHealth are still evolving.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there are many different criteria that can be used to evaluate user-facing eHealth, however the criteria concepts are similar across studies.
the field of eHealth evaluation is moving forward, with a clear focus on the user experience.
there is a growing consensus on the key concepts that should be considered in the evaluation of user-focused eHealth products.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the field of eHealth evaluation is maturing.
a large proportion of criteria are still not well-defined and are therefore not suitable to be used as a checklist.
the evaluation of eHealth programs should be based on a comprehensive set of criteria that are aligned with the program’s goals and objectives.
